description: The Revolt of 1857 was the first major armed struggle against the rule of the British East India Company in India. It is widely known as the First War of Indian Independence, the Sepoy Mutiny, and the Great Rebellion.

sections.title: Causes of the Revolt
sections.description: The rebellion was the culmination of multi-faceted grievances encompassing political, economic, socio-religious, and military aspects of British rule.

key_concepts.explanation: An annexation policy devised by Lord Dalhousie, stating that any princely state under the direct or indirect control of the East India Company would be annexed if the ruler did not have a legal male heir (e.g., Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur).

A rumor spread among the sepoys that the grease used in the new Enfield rifle cartridges was made of cow and pig fat. Biting off the cartridge paper violated the religious sentiments of both Hindu and Muslim soldiers, becoming the immediate cause of the revolt.

Passed by Lord Canning, this act mandated all future recruits of the Bengal Army to serve anywhere the British government required, including overseas. Crossing the sea (Kala Pani) was considered a loss of caste for orthodox Hindus.

sections.title: Outbreak and Key Events
sections.description: The revolt began as a mutiny of sepoys in military cantonments and rapidly escalated into a civilian rebellion across North and Central India.

historical_events.significance: Mangal Pandey, a sepoy of the 34th Native Infantry, refused to use the greased cartridges and attacked his British officers (Sergeant Major Hewson and Adjutant Baugh). He was hanged on April 8, 1857.

Sepoys of the 3rd Native Cavalry at Meerut broke into open revolt, freed their imprisoned comrades, killed British officers, and marched towards Delhi. This is considered the official outbreak of the revolt.
The mutineers captured Delhi and proclaimed the aging Mughal Emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, as the 'Emperor of India' (Shahenshah-e-Hindustan), making him the symbolic leader of the revolt.

sections.title: Key Leaders and Centers of Revolt
sections.description: The revolt was led by various local rulers, deposed nobility, and regional commanders who had their own grievances against the British.

key_associations.associated_with: Bahadur Shah Zafar & General Bakht Khan
key_associations.extra_info: Bahadur Shah was the nominal head, while the actual military command was in the hands of General Bakht Khan, a former subedar of artillery.
Nana Saheb was the adopted son of the last Peshwa, Baji Rao II. The British had refused to grant him his father's pension.
Wife of the deposed Nawab of Awadh (Wajid Ali Shah). She declared her minor son, Birjis Qadir, as the Nawab and organized an armed rebellion against the British.
She rebelled because Lord Dalhousie refused to recognize her adopted son, Damodar Rao, as the legal heir to the throne of Jhansi under the Doctrine of Lapse.
An 80-year-old Rajput zamindar who actively led the rebellion in Bihar, defeating the British forces multiple times before succumbing to injuries.

sections.title: Suppression of the Revolt
sections.description: The British eventually crushed the rebellion with superior military tactics, modern weapons, and the support of loyal Indian contingents (like Gurkhas and Sikhs).

key_associations.extra_info: Nicholson was killed during the siege. Hodson captured Bahadur Shah Zafar and brutally executed his sons in cold blood at Khooni Darwaza.
Commander-in-Chief of the British forces who successfully recaptured both cities with the help of Gurkha regiments.
He defeated Rani Lakshmibai and famously remarked that she was 'the only man among the mutineers' due to her exceptional bravery.

important_facts.fact: Lord Canning was the Governor-General of India during the Revolt of 1857.
Lord Palmerston was the Prime Minister of Britain during the outbreak of the revolt.
After being captured, Bahadur Shah Zafar was tried for treason and exiled to Rangoon (Myanmar), where he died in 1862, ending the Mughal dynasty.

sections.title: Impact and Consequences
sections.description: The failure of the revolt completely transformed the administrative and military structure of British India.

key_concepts.explanation: A commission appointed to reorganize the Indian Army post-1857. It drastically increased the ratio of European to Indian soldiers and ensured that artillery and crucial weapons were kept exclusively in European hands.

historical_events.significance: Abolished the rule of the British East India Company and transferred control of India directly to the British Crown. The designation of Governor-General was changed to Viceroy of India.

Read out by Lord Canning at the Allahabad Darbar. It officially abandoned the Doctrine of Lapse, promised respect for the rights of native princes, and pledged non-interference in Indian religious practices.

sections.title: Books and Views on the Revolt
sections.description: Historians and prominent personalities have interpreted the nature of the 1857 revolt in vastly different ways.

key_associations.extra_info: He was the first to term the revolt as a planned 'First War of Indian Independence' rather than a mere sepoy mutiny.

key_associations.extra_info: He famously concluded that the revolt was 'neither first, nor national, nor a war of independence'.
